summary: This best current practice recommends that networks give general-purpose end hosts multiple global IPv6 addresses when they attach. It describes the benefits of doing so and the options for how a network can provide them. The aim is to make it easy for hosts to use several addresses, for example for different purposes.

eli5.summary: Instead of giving each computer just one house number, the network can give it several, so it can use a different one for different jobs. This says networks should do that and shows how.

questions: why give hosts multiple ipv6 addresses
how many ipv6 addresses should a host get
should ipv6 networks use dhcpv6 or slaac
what is ipv6 nat66 and why avoid it
subtitle: Why IPv6 networks should hand each host many addresses instead of just one.

tldr.problem: Network designers often carry the IPv4 habit of one address per host into IPv6, even though IPv6 addresses are not scarce. Limiting a host to one address breaks features that need more than one and pushes hosts toward NAT.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends that networks give general-purpose hosts multiple IPv6 addresses from each prefix, without needing an explicit request. It lists three ways to do that: SLAAC, stateful DHCPv6 and DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice with no protocol changes. Its advice is to avoid hard limits on the address pool and to prefer SLAAC or a dedicated /64 prefix per host.

Typical need for a multi-function host

today: RFC 7934 is a Best Current Practice and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It changes no protocol: it is operational advice for networks that attach general-purpose hosts.

sections.title: Thinking of IPv6 as Bigger IPv4
sections.content:
IPv6 is similar to IPv4 in most ways, so designers tend to treat it as 128-bit IPv4 and reuse the same configurations. That is usually good, because it eases the transition and the running of dual-stack networks. In host addressing it is a trap.

IPv4 addresses are scarce, so networks hand out one per host. IPv6 addresses are not scarce: a single link offers over four billion times more address space than the whole IPv4 Internet. Giving a host only one address wastes benefits such as application simplicity, privacy and the ability to offer Internet access without Network Address Translation (NAT).

The document does not change any protocol or host behavior. It lists the benefits of multiple addresses, the problems of restricting them, and the options for providing them.
sections.eli5: A town with billions of house numbers does not need to give each family only one. This document reminds network builders that IPv6 has plenty of numbers to share.

sections.title: Why Hosts Need More Than One Address
sections.content:
IPv6 is designed to support several global addresses per interface. Many hosts already use three or more: a link-local address, a stable address, one or more privacy addresses, and possibly addresses from DHCPv6. In most general-purpose networks a host can form extra addresses from the link prefix without asking the network, which holds for all 3GPP networks as well as Ethernet and Wi-Fi networks using SLAAC.

Several functions need more than one address: privacy addressing, multiple processors in one device (such as an application processor and a baseband processor), tethering, virtual machines, translation-based transition technologies such as 464XLAT, identifier-locator addressing, and future applications such as per-application addresses.

Two examples show new applications deployed without asking the network. 464XLAT can run even when the NAT64 service is provided by a different network than the residential ISP, because the ISP lets users obtain the extra IPv6 address. And /64 sharing lets a phone offer IPv6 tethering without waiting for operators to deploy DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation.
sections.eli5: One computer may be doing many jobs at once, like a phone sharing its connection with a laptop. Each job is easier if it can have its own address, like each person in a house having their own mailbox.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong When Addresses Are Limited
sections.content:
If a network gives only a limited number of addresses, functions that need more are either unavailable or only work after an explicit request to the network is granted. The RFC lists the costs of such requests: added latency (possibly including human intervention to update a service agreement), uncertainty about whether a feature will work, complexity from handling failures and timeouts, and more load on provisioning servers.

Operators may still want limits for reasons such as hardware limits (Ternary Content-Addressable Memory size or Neighbor Cache size), business models that charge per device, or consistency with IPv4 address management. The RFC argues that hardware limits are expected to ease, and that charging per device may backfire if customers respond with NAT, as they did with IPv4, leaving no extra revenue but more operational problems and support costs.

Hosts can mostly get around limits by running NAT on the host (NAT66). NAT makes applications more complex because of NAT traversal, hinders new applications, and hurts battery life through frequent keepalives. UDP applications that must work on most of the Internet have to send keepalives at least every 30 seconds, and QUIC uses a 15-second keepalive. The IAB guidance is that IPv6 NAT is not desirable, yet NAT66 already exists in client operating systems: Linux has supported it since 2012.
sections.eli5: If you must ask the office for a new mailbox every time you need one, everything is slow and sometimes the answer is no. Kids then invent workarounds, which make a mess for everybody.

sections.title: Three Ways to Provide Multiple Addresses
sections.content:
SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) lets hosts create global addresses on demand from the prefixes assigned to the link. It is typically used on shared links, but can also be used with a dedicated /64 per host, for example on point-to-point 3GPP links, per-host VLANs, or wireless networks that put each MAC address in its own broadcast domain.

Stateful DHCPv6 address assignment can give multiple temporary and non-temporary addresses, though most clients ask for only one non-temporary address. With a typical MTU of 1500 bytes or smaller, about 30 addresses is the maximum in a single DHCPv6 packet.

DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (PD) delegates a prefix to the client, which forms its own addresses from it. A prefix shorter than /64 can be split into subnets. A /64 can be extended through L2 bridging, ND proxying or /64 sharing, but cannot be subdivided because a prefix longer than /64 is outside the current IPv6 specifications. PD does not require the client to be a router, although hosts that tether or run virtual machines often already forward packets.

sections.eli5: There are three ways to get lots of mailbox numbers. Make them up yourself within a street, ask the office for a list, or ask the office for a whole street of your own.

sections.title: The Recommendations
sections.content:
Section 7 notes that it is not possible to estimate in advance how many addresses a host needs. Privacy addresses can use up to 7 addresses, one per day. A mobile device sharing its uplink may support 8 downstream devices. Add virtual machines, 464XLAT and a baseband chip, and even a host doing a few of these might need on the order of 20 addresses at once.

The RFC therefore says:

  • Networks RECOMMENDED to provide multiple IPv6 addresses from each prefix to general-purpose hosts.
  • It is NOT RECOMMENDED to impose a hard limit on the host's address pool, and particularly not to limit a host to one IPv6 address per prefix.
  • It is RECOMMENDED that the host can use new addresses without explicit requests, either by forming them itself (for example with SLAAC) or by getting a dedicated /64 prefix. That prefix MAY come from DHCPv6 PD, SLAAC with per-device VLANs, or other means.

Stateful DHCPv6 assignment of about 30 addresses at connection time would serve current clients, but it sets a limit and so limits the development of future applications.
sections.eli5: The rule is: do not set a small fixed limit on addresses, and do not make hosts beg for each one. Let them make their own, or give them a whole street.

sections.title: Operational Concerns
sections.content:
Host tracking. Some operators must log which address belongs to which host. The RFC says this does not need DHCPv6: operators can monitor the router Neighbor Cache through SNMP or logging. With SLAAC and a dedicated /64 per host, only the assigned prefix needs logging. It also notes that DHCPv6 does not guarantee reliable tracking, since on a shared network without L2 edge port security hosts can choose their own addresses. Mechanisms such as SAVI can enforce address use and are more reliable than server logs.

Address space. A network that fits in 192.168.0.0/16 in IPv4 maps to a /48 in IPv6, giving each host a /64. A network using 10.0.0.0/8 maps to a /40. The RFC says these are easy to obtain under current RIR policies. Residential users typically get a /48, /56 or /60 and use SLAAC, so they pose no particular limit on host addresses.

Link scalability. Each (L2, IP) address pair costs router and switch memory, MLD snooping state and solicited node multicast groups. Hosts creating hundreds or thousands of addresses may find their access restricted by denial-of-service protection. A dedicated /64 per host, especially via DHCPv6 PD, means one routing entry and one ND cache entry per host, though it uses more address space.
sections.eli5: Network staff worry about keeping track of who is who and about not overloading the equipment. Giving each computer its own street keeps the records simple and the equipment relaxed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
On shared networks using SLAAC, a host could try to exhaust network resources and deny service to others by creating an unreasonable number of addresses, for example hundreds or thousands. Networks serving untrusted hosts can mitigate this by giving each host a dedicated /64 prefix.

Another mitigation is limiting the number of Neighbor Cache entries per host, but care is needed so legitimate multi-address hosts are not blocked. Tracking-related security issues are covered in the host tracking discussion.
sections.eli5: A naughty computer could make up so many addresses that the network gets overwhelmed. Giving each untrusted computer its own street stops it from bothering the neighbors.
